newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt, Israel begin talks to revive Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: Egypt, Israel begin talks to revive Mideast peace.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday for crucial talks on the deadlocked Middle East peace process that were expected to focus on Jewish settlements on Arab lands.
Mubarak and Netanyahu chatted in the sunny salon of a hotel in this Egyptian Red Sea resort while Egyptian Foreign Minister held separate talks with Israeli counterpart David Levy.

Egypt had made clear it would speak for the Palestinians. Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, who held talks with Mubarak in Cairo on Monday, said he hoped the summit would revive peace negotiations stalled since March when Israel broke ground on a new settlement.
"The problem isn't building for Palestinians, rather halting the settlements," Arafat said.
Palestinians refuse to resume talks unless Israel stops building the settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, part of the West Bank occupied by Israel in 1967.
Asked if he would meet Netanyahu if construction ceased, Arafat told reporters in Gaza: "The most important thing is what will happen today between President Mubarak and Mr. Netanyahu."

Moussa said settlements would be the issue at Tuesday's summit but Netanyahu had said the topic was not on his agenda for the meeting. The prime minister's spokesman brushed aside the significance of the Jerusalem settlement to peace.

"There are very important issues that we have to discuss. This is a discussion of the destinies of two people in a very small piece of land and that should be addressed, not details like whether there is going to be a housing project here or a housing project there," David Bar-Illan said in Sharm el-Sheikh.
"To make that housing project an obstacle to peace is really to mock the peace process," he told reporters.

In remarks to Israel's daily Haaretz, Arafat forecast a "disaster" unless there was progress in peacemaking. Moussa had said he hoped Netanyahu would change his mind about the settlement for the sake of peace.

"The Palestinians say they cannot negotiate against a background of fait accomplis and the continuation of settlements. Our job is to deal with that in order to pave the way for the resumption of a positive atmosphere which will enable us to save the peace process," Moussa said on Monday.
The U.S. ambassador to Israel also said he did not expect breakthroughs at the Egypt meeting but Israel's Levy said he hoped the meeting would help break the impasse.

"We are making a joint effort to solve matters. I hope we will succeed. Of course it doesn't depend on Israel alone but on both sides. It is an important meeting and I hope the result also will be important," Levy said on arrival in Egypt.
Egyptian newspapers were sceptical the summit would produce progress and blamed Netanyahu for the crisis.
"We're not very optimistic about dealing with him because Netanyahu is the reason behind the deterioration in the peace process," Saeed Sonbol, senior editor at al-Akhar daily said in his column.
